## What this is

DataMimic fits a generative model to a table and draws new rows from it. The
synthetic rows are not copies or perturbations of real ones — they are samples
from a distribution estimated from your data, so column distributions and the
relationships between columns survive while individual records do not.

This document is a deep dive rather than a quickstart. It works through four
real datasets spanning different shapes of tabular problem, and opens up each
method far enough to explain how it works and where it fails. If you only want
to generate a table, the [README](https://github.com/mthelm85/DataMimic.jl) is
shorter and enough.

It also ends somewhere I did not expect when I started writing it, which is
left in rather than tidied away — see [Choosing an engine,
empirically](#choosing-an-engine-empirically).

Everything here executes. If a number in the text disagrees with the output
below it, trust the output.

### Running it yourself

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mthelm85/DataMimic.jl
cd DataMimic.jl
quarto render notebooks/guided-tour.qmd
```

The datasets download on first run (about 60 MB, mostly Covertype) and cache
under `benchmark/data/`. A full render takes roughly half an hour, most of it
the two diffusion models trained in [How diffusion works](#how-diffusion-works)
— everything else finishes in seconds.

```{julia}
using DataMimic
using DataFrames, Random, Statistics, Printf
using CairoMakie
using Lux, Zygote          # activates the DiffusionGenerator extension

include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "benchmark", "datasets.jl"))

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
set_theme!(theme_minimal(); fontsize = 12,
           Axis = (; xgridvisible = false, topspinevisible = false,
                     rightspinevisible = false))

const PALETTE = (real = "#3B6EA5", synth = "#C1666B", accent = "#6A8D73")
Random.seed!(20250831)
nothing
```

## The four datasets

Each one is a different *shape* of tabular problem, and the shape is what
decides which engine suits it.

```{julia}
adult  = load_adult()
german = load_german_credit()
wine   = load_wine(colour = :white)
cover  = load_covertype(n = 30_000)

function shape_row(name, df, note)
    num = count(c -> eltype(df[!, c]) <: Union{Missing, Number}, names(df))
    (dataset = name, rows = nrow(df), cols = ncol(df),
     numeric = num, categorical = ncol(df) - num,
     missings = sum(sum(ismissing, df[!, c]) for c in names(df)),
     character = note)
end

DataFrame([
    shape_row("Adult",         adult,  "mixed, has missing values"),
    shape_row("German Credit", german, "small, categorical-heavy"),
    shape_row("Wine Quality",  wine,   "entirely continuous"),
    shape_row("Covertype",     cover,  "large, continuous + binary"),
])
```

The conventional reading of that table would go something like this:

| Dataset | Shape | Might expect | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adult | mixed, 48k rows | `DiffusionGenerator` | enough rows to train a network on mixed types |
| German Credit | 1k rows, 14 categorical | `MSTGenerator` | discrete data is what contingency tables are for |
| Wine | 4.9k rows, all continuous | `DPCopulaGenerator` | a covariance matrix is a natural summary here |
| Covertype | 30k rows, mostly numeric | varies with row count | large enough that private engines recover their signal |

Every one of those is a hypothesis about which engine suits which shape, and
they are the kind of thing that gets asserted in documentation without being
checked. The last section checks them. Two do not survive.

## Your first synthetic table

Everything goes through `fit` and `sample`.

```{julia}
model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult; rng = MersenneTwister(1))
syn   = sample(model, nrow(adult); rng = MersenneTwister(2))

first(syn, 5)
```

`fit` accepts any [Tables.jl](https://github.com/JuliaData/Tables.jl) source and
`sample` returns the same concrete type, so a `DataFrame` in gives a
`DataFrame` out. You can draw more rows than you started with.

### What `fit` decided about your columns

Before any modelling, every column is classified. The classification drives
everything downstream, so it is worth looking at.

```{julia}
DataFrame(column = Symbol.(names(adult)),
          kind = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(adult[!, c]) for c in names(adult)],
          distinct = [length(unique(skipmissing(adult[!, c]))) for c in names(adult)])
```

Two of those deserve comment.

`:fnlwgt` is a census sampling weight — a large integer with very high
cardinality. `:education_num` is an integer encoding of `:education`, so the
two columns are perfectly redundant.

Detection is **cardinality-aware**, which matters most for integers. A column
of whole numbers holding five distinct values in fifty thousand rows is a
category that happens to be numbered, and modelling it as continuous would
invent values between the levels. The same column with fifty thousand distinct
values is a genuine numeric variable. The line is drawn by the ratio of
distinct values to rows, not by the element type.

When that inference gets it wrong, override it:

```{julia}
hinted = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult;
             hints = [ColumnHint(name = :education_num, kind = :categorical)],
             rng = MersenneTwister(1))
nothing
```

### Missing values

Adult codes missing entries as `?`, which the loader turns into `missing`.

```{julia}
miss = DataFrame(column = names(adult),
                 real_missing = [sum(ismissing, adult[!, c]) for c in names(adult)],
                 synth_missing = [sum(ismissing, syn[!, c]) for c in names(syn)])
filter(r -> r.real_missing > 0, miss)
```

Missingness is measured per column at fit time and reintroduced at the same
rate when sampling, so the synthetic table has a comparable missingness profile
rather than a suspiciously complete one.

The *rate* is modelled, not the *pattern*: whether a value is missing is drawn
independently per cell. If missingness in your data is correlated across
columns — a block of questions skipped together — that structure is not
reproduced. Worth knowing before you use synthetic data to study nonresponse.

### Did it work?

The first thing to look at is whether the marginals line up.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Real and synthetic marginals for four Adult columns."
function marginal_panel(real_df, syn_df, cols; nbins = 40)
    fig = Figure(size = (900, 480))
    for (i, c) in enumerate(cols)
        r = collect(skipmissing(real_df[!, c]))
        s = collect(skipmissing(syn_df[!, c]))
        ax = Axis(fig[fldmod1(i, 2)...]; title = string(c))
        if eltype(r) <: Number
            lo, hi = extrema(vcat(Float64.(r), Float64.(s)))
            edges = range(lo, hi; length = nbins)
            hist!(ax, Float64.(r); bins = edges, normalization = :pdf,
                  color = (PALETTE.real, 0.55), label = "real")
            hist!(ax, Float64.(s); bins = edges, normalization = :pdf,
                  color = (PALETTE.synth, 0.55), label = "synthetic")
        else
            levs = sort(unique(vcat(string.(r), string.(s))))
            pr = [count(==(l), string.(r)) / length(r) for l in levs]
            ps = [count(==(l), string.(s)) / length(s) for l in levs]
            barplot!(ax, (1:length(levs)) .- 0.2, pr; width = 0.4,
                     color = (PALETTE.real, 0.8), label = "real")
            barplot!(ax, (1:length(levs)) .+ 0.2, ps; width = 0.4,
                     color = (PALETTE.synth, 0.8), label = "synthetic")
            ax.xticks = (1:length(levs), levs)
            ax.xticklabelrotation = π / 4
            ax.xticklabelsize = 9
        end
        i == 1 && axislegend(ax; position = :rt, framevisible = false, labelsize = 10)
    end
    fig
end

marginal_panel(adult, syn, [:age, :hours_per_week, :education, :sex])
```

Marginals matching is necessary but nowhere near sufficient — a generator that
sampled every column independently would pass this test and be useless. The
[Evaluation](#evaluation-what-the-numbers-mean) section takes that apart
properly.

## How the copula works

Wine Quality is the clearest place to see this: eleven continuous, strongly
correlated measurements and nothing else.

A **copula** separates a joint distribution into two independent parts: each
column's own marginal distribution, and the dependence structure linking them.
Sklar's theorem says this decomposition always exists — for any joint CDF $F$
with marginals $F_1, \dots, F_d$ there is a copula $C$ such that

$$
F(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C\bigl(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\bigr),
$$

and $C$ is unique wherever the marginals are continuous. That is a strong fit
for tabular data: each column's shape is captured *exactly* by its empirical
distribution, and only the coupling has to be estimated.

### Step 1 — the probability integral transform

Push each column through its own empirical CDF. Whatever shape it had becomes
uniform on $[0,1]$, and only the ranks survive.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Left: two Wine columns as measured. Right: the same rows after the rank transform. The marginals are gone; the dependence is not."
function pit(v)
    r = sortperm(sortperm(v))
    (r .- 0.5) ./ length(v)
end

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "residual sugar", ylabel = "density",
           title = "original scale")
scatter!(ax1, wine.residual_sugar, wine.density;
         color = (PALETTE.real, 0.25), markersize = 4)
ylims!(ax1, 0.985, 1.005)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "F(residual sugar)", ylabel = "F(density)",
           title = "pseudo-observations")
scatter!(ax2, pit(wine.residual_sugar), pit(wine.density);
         color = (PALETTE.accent, 0.25), markersize = 4)
fig
```

The right-hand panel is what the copula actually models. Both axes are uniform
by construction, so nothing about the marginal shapes remains — the visible
structure is pure dependence.

To sample, DataMimic draws from the fitted copula and pushes each coordinate
back through the corresponding inverse CDF. The marginals come back exactly
right by construction, which is why copula output looks so plausible
column-by-column.

### Step 2 — does the dependence survive?

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Spearman correlation of Wine Quality: real, synthetic, and the difference."
function spearman_matrix(df, cols)
    R = hcat([pit(Float64.(df[!, c])) for c in cols]...)
    cor(R)
end

wine_cols = Symbol.(names(wine))
wine_model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), wine; rng = MersenneTwister(3))
wine_syn   = sample(wine_model, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(4))

Cr = spearman_matrix(wine, wine_cols)
Cs = spearman_matrix(wine_syn, wine_cols)

# Wine's column names are long; abbreviate them so the ticks stay readable.
short(c) = join(first.(split(string(c), "_")), "") * "." *
           last(split(string(c), "_"))[1:min(3, length(last(split(string(c), "_"))))]
labels = [short(c) for c in wine_cols]

function corr_axis(pos, M, ttl, range_; ylabels)
    ax = Axis(pos; title = ttl, aspect = 1,
              xticks = (1:length(labels), labels),
              yticks = (1:length(labels), ylabels ? labels : fill("", length(labels))),
              xticklabelrotation = π / 2,
              xticklabelsize = 8, yticklabelsize = 8)
    heatmap!(ax, M; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = range_)
end

fig = Figure(size = (1040, 420))
corr_axis(fig[1, 1], Cr, "real",      (-1, 1); ylabels = true)
corr_axis(fig[1, 2], Cs, "synthetic", (-1, 1); ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 3]; colormap = :RdBu, limits = (-1, 1),
         width = 10, label = "ρ", ticklabelsize = 9)
hm = corr_axis(fig[1, 4], Cs .- Cr, "difference (5× tighter scale)",
               (-0.2, 0.2); ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 5], hm; width = 10, label = "Δρ", ticklabelsize = 9)
colgap!(fig.layout, 8)
fig
```

The third panel is the one that matters: it is the error, on a five-times
tighter colour scale than the first two.

```{julia}
@printf("max |Δρ| = %.3f   mean |Δρ| = %.3f\n",
        maximum(abs.(Cs .- Cr)), mean(abs.(Cs .- Cr)))
```

### Step 3 — categoricals, and why `:beta` beats `:gaussian`

A copula wants continuous marginals, and a categorical column has none. The way
in is the **distributional transform**: a level occupying the CDF interval
$[F(k-1), F(k)]$ maps to a uniform draw *inside* that interval, and sampling
inverts the same step function. Dependence between categorical and numeric
columns is then modelled rather than discarded.

Two consequences follow, and they explain the two copula families' very
different behaviour.

The association a copula can express is **monotone in the level ordering**, and
for a nominal variable that ordering is arbitrary — `occupation` has no natural
sequence. So this captures a substantial part of the dependence, not all of it.
And a Gaussian copula has only a correlation matrix to work with, so it can
*only* express monotone dependence; the nonparametric Beta copula can represent
the non-monotone structure an arbitrary ordering produces.

On a mixed table that difference is large:

```{julia}
sub = adult[1:8000, [:age, :education, :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]
holdout = adult[8001:14000, names(sub)]

function utility_of(gen, data, test; seed = 5)
    m = fit(gen, data; rng = MersenneTwister(seed))
    s = sample(m, nrow(data); rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 1))
    utility_tstr(data, s, :income; test = test, rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 2))
end

beta_u  = utility_of(CopulaGenerator(:beta),     sub, holdout)
gauss_u = utility_of(CopulaGenerator(:gaussian), sub, holdout)

DataFrame(copula = ["beta", "gaussian"],
          synth_f1 = [beta_u.synth_score, gauss_u.synth_score],
          real_f1  = [beta_u.real_score,  gauss_u.real_score],
          ratio    = [beta_u.ratio,       gauss_u.ratio])
```

`:beta` is the default for exactly this reason. Reach for `:gaussian` when you
specifically want a Gaussian dependence structure, not as a faster option.

### What a copula cannot do

It is worth being precise about the limits, because copulas are otherwise so
well-behaved that it is easy to over-trust them.

- **Dependence is pairwise.** A copula fitted this way captures the coupling
  between pairs of columns. Genuine three-way interactions — a relationship
  between A and B that reverses depending on C — are not represented.
- **Nominal ordering is arbitrary**, as above.
- **A single-level column** cannot be encoded at all, so it is left out of the
  copula and drawn independently.

When those limits bind, a diffusion model is the escape hatch, and it is where
we go next.

## How diffusion works

A copula assumes the dependence structure has a particular form. A diffusion
model assumes almost nothing and learns it, at the cost of needing many more
rows and a great deal more compute.

The idea: destroy the data with noise in small steps until nothing is left,
train a network to undo *one* step, and then generate by starting from noise
and running that reversal all the way back.

### The forward process

For numeric columns this is the standard DDPM construction. Given a variance
schedule $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_T$ and $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1-\beta_s)$,
you can jump to any timestep in one shot:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I}\bigr).
$$

So $\bar\alpha_t$ is the whole story: it is how much of the original signal
survives to step $t$. DataMimic uses the cosine schedule, which spends far more
of its budget in the region where the signal is actually being destroyed.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Cosine vs linear schedules. The cosine schedule destroys signal gradually rather than collapsing it early."
const Ext = Base.get_extension(DataMimic, :DataMimicLuxExt)

T = 100
betas_cos, _ = Ext._cosine_schedule(T)
sched_cos = Ext._schedule_constants(betas_cos)
betas_lin = collect(range(1e-4, 0.02; length = T))
ac_lin = cumprod(1 .- betas_lin)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 340))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "timestep t", ylabel = "ᾱₜ  (signal retained)",
           title = "how much of x₀ survives")
lines!(ax1, 1:T, sched_cos.alphas_cumprod; color = PALETTE.real, linewidth = 2.5,
       label = "cosine (used)")
lines!(ax1, 1:T, ac_lin; color = PALETTE.synth, linewidth = 2.5,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "linear")
axislegend(ax1; framevisible = false)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "timestep t", ylabel = "βₜ",
           title = "per-step noise added")
lines!(ax2, 1:T, betas_cos; color = PALETTE.real, linewidth = 2.5)
lines!(ax2, 1:T, betas_lin; color = PALETTE.synth, linewidth = 2.5, linestyle = :dash)
fig
```

Watching a real column dissolve makes the process concrete:

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "One Adult column pushed forward through the diffusion process. By t = 100 it is indistinguishable from noise."
x0 = Float32.((adult.age .- mean(adult.age)) ./ std(adult.age))[1:4000]
fig = Figure(size = (960, 240))
for (j, t) in enumerate([1, 20, 50, 100])
    ab = sched_cos.alphas_cumprod[t]
    xt = sqrt(ab) .* x0 .+ sqrt(1 - ab) .* randn(MersenneTwister(t), Float32, length(x0))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t   (ᾱ = $(round(ab; digits = 3)))",
              yticksvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false)
    hist!(ax, xt; bins = 50, color = (PALETTE.accent, 0.7), normalization = :pdf)
    xlims!(ax, -4, 4)
end
fig
```

### The reverse process, and what the network learns

Training samples a random $t$ per row, noises that row to step $t$, and asks
the network to predict the noise $\varepsilon$ that was added. The objective is
plain mean squared error, $\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon - \hat\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2$,
which is a reparametrization of the variational bound.

Categorical columns cannot be noised with Gaussians, so TabDDPM runs a **second
diffusion process in parallel over the same timestep**. Multinomial diffusion
interpolates each one-hot vector toward the uniform distribution over its
levels:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathrm{Cat}\bigl(x_t;\ (1-\beta_t)\,x_{t-1} + \beta_t/K\bigr),
$$

and the categorical part of the loss is the KL between the true posterior
$q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)$ and the model's. That matters: categorical structure
is modelled *as* categorical rather than embedded in a continuous space and
rounded back, which is where many tabular generators lose discrete
relationships.

The whole thing is carried in **log space**, because probabilities for a
42-level column at $t = 100$ underflow Float32 otherwise.

### Training one, and what a small budget buys

```{julia}
adult_sub = adult[1:20_000, [:age, :workclass, :education, :marital_status,
                             :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]

function train_diffusion(epochs)
    gen = DiffusionGenerator(
        epochs        = epochs,
        batch_size    = 4096,
        d_layers      = [256, 512, 512, 256],
        num_timesteps = 100,
        target        = :income,          # class-conditional
    )
    t0 = time()
    m = fit(gen, adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(11))
    s = sample(m, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(12))
    (; epochs, model = m, syn = s, secs = time() - t0,
       fidelity = fidelity_score(adult_sub, s).aggregate,
       tstr = utility_tstr(adult_sub, s, :income; rng = MersenneTwister(15)).ratio)
end

runs = [train_diffusion(60), train_diffusion(200)]
diff_model, diff_syn = runs[end].model, runs[end].syn

cop_m = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(13))
cop_s = sample(cop_m, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(14))

DataFrame(
    engine   = ["CopulaGenerator", "Diffusion (60 epochs)", "Diffusion (200 epochs)"],
    fidelity = [fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s).aggregate,
                runs[1].fidelity, runs[2].fidelity],
    tstr     = [utility_tstr(adult_sub, cop_s, :income;
                             rng = MersenneTwister(15)).ratio,
                runs[1].tstr, runs[2].tstr],
    fit_secs = [NaN, runs[1].secs, runs[2].secs],
)
```

Naming a `target` column switches on **class-conditional** generation: the
denoiser is conditioned on an embedding of the label, and labels are drawn from
the empirical class distribution at sampling time. On classification-style
tables this markedly improves downstream utility, and it reproduces the paper's
own setup.

**The copula wins here, decisively, and that is the point.** These diffusion
runs are badly undertrained — 200 epochs over 20,000 rows at batch 4096 is
about a thousand optimizer steps, where the paper's Adult configuration uses
several thousand on a network roughly four times wider. What the table does
show is the *direction*: fidelity improves substantially from 60 to 200 epochs
while the copula stays put, because the copula was already converged after a
few seconds.

That is the single most common way to misread a comparison like this one.
A `DiffusionGenerator` left at a small epoch count is measuring your patience,
not the method — which is why the practical guidance later says to give every
engine a fair configuration before drawing conclusions. The tuned setup lives
in `benchmark/eval_tstr.jl`; it takes considerably longer than a document
should.

You can see the undertraining directly in the numeric columns:

```{julia}
DataFrame(column = [:age, :hours_per_week],
          real_sd  = [std(adult_sub.age), std(adult_sub.hours_per_week)],
          synth_sd = [std(diff_syn.age),  std(diff_syn.hours_per_week)])
```

The reverse process divides by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, which for a 100-step
cosine schedule reaches the order of $10^3$ at the noisiest steps. That
amplifies any error in the predicted noise by the same factor, so an
imperfectly trained model produces numeric columns that are far too dispersed —
and, in the worst case, rows that overflow to `Inf` entirely.

::: {.callout-note}
## Rejection sampling is not free

DataMimic discards rows whose numeric block comes back non-finite and redraws
them. That is what the reference implementation does, but it is worth being
explicit that **it is not distribution-preserving**: keeping only the rows that
survive samples from the distribution *conditioned on finiteness*, and
divergence is not independent of the data. For a class-conditional model it
correlates with the label, because the label is an input to the denoiser.

So the discard rate is tracked, a warning is raised when any rows are dropped,
and past a threshold `sample` refuses to return the result rather than hand
back a biased table that nothing downstream would flag.
:::

## Differential privacy

Everything so far preserves structure without copying records, which is useful
but is *not* a guarantee. A determined attacker can still ask whether a
particular person was in the training data, and nothing above stops them
answering.

Differential privacy does. A mechanism is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially
private if for any two tables differing in one record, and any set of outputs
$S$,

$$
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta .
$$

Concretely: had one person been removed before fitting, the probability of
producing any particular synthetic dataset would change by at most a factor of
about $e^{\varepsilon}$. Nobody can confidently determine whether a given
individual was in the input — no matter what auxiliary information they bring,
and no matter what is published later.

### MST, step by step

German Credit is the natural home for `MSTGenerator`: a thousand rows, mostly
categorical, and genuinely sensitive.

MST won the NIST differential privacy synthetic data challenge, and it is built
on one observation — you cannot afford to measure everything privately, so
spend the budget on the relationships that matter most.

```{julia}
budget = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0, delta = 1e-5)
mst_model = fit(MSTGenerator(), german; privacy = budget, rng = MersenneTwister(21))
mst_syn   = sample(mst_model, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(22))
first(mst_syn, 4)
```

What just happened, in six steps:

1. **Discretize.** Every column is binned — numeric columns into 32 equal-width
   bins by default — because the algorithm works over contingency tables.
2. **Measure all one-way marginals** under Gaussian noise. There are only as
   many as there are columns, so they are cheap, and they anchor each column's
   own distribution.
3. **Select a spanning tree.** Each candidate pair is scored by how badly the
   independence assumption fails for it, and a maximum spanning tree over
   columns is chosen with the **exponential mechanism**, which makes the
   selection itself private. A tree, rather than an arbitrary graph, is what
   keeps the next step exact.
4. **Measure the selected two-way marginals** under Gaussian noise.
5. **Reconcile.** The noisy measurements are mutually inconsistent — one
   marginal's implied column totals will not match another's. Private-PGM fits
   a single tree-structured graphical model that best explains all of them at
   once, by entropic mirror descent over the marginal polytope with exact
   belief propagation for inference.
6. **Sample** ancestrally from the reconciled model, then map bins back to
   values.

Step 5 is **post-processing**: it touches only already-private measurements, so
it costs no budget at all. That is a genuine property of differential privacy,
not a loophole.

Here is the tree the algorithm actually chose:

```{julia}
edges = [(string(mst_model.stat_columns[p]), string(mst_model.stat_columns[c]))
         for (p, c) in mst_model.tree_edges]
DataFrame(parent = first.(edges), child = last.(edges))
```

Because selection is private, the tree is itself a random variable: a different
seed gives a different tree. It should be read as "one plausible dependency
skeleton", never as a discovered causal structure.

### What a budget costs

The only way to choose $\varepsilon$ for a given dataset is to measure what it
costs there.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Privacy–utility tradeoff on German Credit. Lower fidelity is better; higher utility is better."
eps_grid = [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]

fid_sweep = privacy_utility_sweep(MSTGenerator(), german, eps_grid,
                (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate;
                rng = MersenneTwister(23))
util_sweep = privacy_utility_sweep(MSTGenerator(), german, eps_grid,
                (r, s) -> utility_tstr(r, s, :credit_risk;
                                       rng = MersenneTwister(24)).ratio;
                rng = MersenneTwister(25))

fig = Figure(size = (900, 340))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "ε", ylabel = "fidelity distance",
           title = "fidelity (lower is better)", xticks = (eps_grid, string.(eps_grid)))
lines!(ax1, eps_grid, [r.metric_result for r in fid_sweep];
       color = PALETTE.real, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax1, eps_grid, [r.metric_result for r in fid_sweep];
         color = PALETTE.real, markersize = 9)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "ε", ylabel = "TSTR ratio",
           title = "utility (higher is better)", xticks = (eps_grid, string.(eps_grid)))
lines!(ax2, eps_grid, [r.metric_result for r in util_sweep];
       color = PALETTE.accent, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax2, eps_grid, [r.metric_result for r in util_sweep];
         color = PALETTE.accent, markersize = 9)
hlines!(ax2, [1.0]; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash)
fig
```

The curve is usually steep at the low end and flat above it, and the useful
question is where *your* data stops improving.

Two things make this harder than it looks. Results at low $\varepsilon$ are
noisy — the seed-to-seed standard deviation of the utility ratio can exceed the
differences you are trying to read — so single curves mislead and several seeds
are needed. And the answer depends on **row count**: at fixed $\varepsilon$ a
private engine improves substantially as rows increase, because its noise is
fixed while the signal grows. A budget that is unusable on a thousand rows may
be comfortable on a hundred thousand.

### How the budget is spent

Each private engine spends its whole budget internally, composing the pieces
under **zero-concentrated differential privacy** (zCDP) and converting to
$(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP at the end. zCDP is used because it composes tightly
across many mechanisms — naive per-step $\varepsilon$ accounting would be far
more pessimistic.

| Engine | Split |
|---|---|
| `MSTGenerator` | 30% tree selection, 20% one-way marginals, 50% two-way marginals |
| `DPCopulaGenerator` | 50% histogram marginals, 50% private covariance |
| `DiffusionGenerator(dp=true)` | DP-SGD, accounted with Rényi DP over Poisson-subsampled minibatches |

### DP-SGD and ghost clipping

DP-SGD clips **each example's** gradient to a fixed norm and then adds Gaussian
noise to the sum. The per-example clipping is what bounds one record's
influence, and it looks like it requires one backward pass per example.

It does not. For a dense layer with inputs $a$ and output-gradients $g$,
example $i$'s weight gradient is the outer product $g_i a_i^\top$, so

$$
\bigl\|\partial L_i / \partial W\bigr\|_F = \|g_i\|\,\|a_i\| ,
$$

a product of two column norms. Summing that across layers gives every example's
gradient norm — hence its clip factor — and the clipped sum is two more
matrix multiplications. Two batched passes replace $B$ unbatched ones. This is
**ghost clipping**, and it is an exact identity rather than an approximation;
DataMimic's test suite asserts the two agree to floating-point rounding.

```{julia}
dp_diff = fit(DiffusionGenerator(dp = true, epochs = 8, batch_size = 512,
                                 d_layers = [128, 128], num_timesteps = 50),
              german; privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 8.0),
              rng = MersenneTwister(26))
dp_syn = sample(dp_diff, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(27))
@printf("fidelity %.4f\n", fidelity_score(german, dp_syn).aggregate)
```

### What differential privacy does not give you

- **Aggregate disclosure.** DP says nothing about whether the *patterns* you
  release are sensitive. A faithfully reproduced correlation can be exactly
  what you did not want to publish.
- **Group privacy.** The guarantee is per-record. Protection for a household,
  or anyone contributing several rows, degrades roughly in proportion to how
  many rows they contribute.
- **Correctness of the input.** The bound concerns the fitting procedure, not
  your right to hold the data.

## Private synthesis of continuous data

Wine is the mirror image of German Credit: entirely continuous, so binning it
into contingency tables throws away most of what makes it interesting.
`DPCopulaGenerator` is the engine for that shape.

It makes both halves of the copula private: differentially private histogram
marginals, and a differentially private covariance matrix estimated by the
**Analyze-Gauss** mechanism.

One implementation detail is worth pulling out, because it is easy to get
wrong and silently halves your noise. The covariance matrix is symmetric, so
noise added to it must be symmetric too — draw the upper triangle and mirror
it. Noising the two triangles independently would give every off-diagonal entry
*half* the intended variance, and the guarantee would not hold.

```{julia}
dpc = fit(DPCopulaGenerator(), wine;
          privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0), rng = MersenneTwister(31))
dpc_syn = sample(dpc, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(32))

DataFrame(engine = ["CopulaGenerator (no privacy)", "DPCopulaGenerator (ε = 1)",
                    "MSTGenerator (ε = 1)"],
          fidelity = [fidelity_score(wine, wine_syn).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(wine, dpc_syn).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(wine, sample(fit(MSTGenerator(), wine;
                          privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0),
                          rng = MersenneTwister(33)), nrow(wine);
                          rng = MersenneTwister(34))).aggregate])
```

On continuous data the DP copula gives up much less than MST does, which is the
whole reason both engines exist.

## What changes at scale

Covertype is large enough to show the effect that matters most for private
synthesis: **more rows buy you utility at no privacy cost**. The noise a
mechanism adds is calibrated to one record's influence, so it does not grow
with $n$ — but the signal does.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "At fixed ε, a private engine improves with row count. A public engine barely moves."
sizes = [1_000, 4_000, 16_000]
rows = NamedTuple[]
for n in sizes
    sub = cover[1:n, :]
    for (label, gen, priv) in (
            ("CopulaGenerator (public)", CopulaGenerator(), nothing),
            ("DPCopulaGenerator (ε=1)", DPCopulaGenerator(), PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0)))
        m = fit(gen, sub; privacy = priv, rng = MersenneTwister(41))
        s = sample(m, n; rng = MersenneTwister(42))
        push!(rows, (n = n, engine = label,
                     fidelity = fidelity_score(sub, s).aggregate))
    end
end
scale_df = DataFrame(rows)

fig = Figure(size = (680, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "rows", ylabel = "fidelity distance",
          title = "fidelity vs row count (lower is better)",
          xticks = (sizes, string.(sizes)))
for (label, col) in (("CopulaGenerator (public)", PALETTE.real),
                     ("DPCopulaGenerator (ε=1)", PALETTE.synth))
    sub = filter(r -> r.engine == label, scale_df)
    lines!(ax, sub.n, sub.fidelity; color = col, linewidth = 2.5, label = label)
    scatter!(ax, sub.n, sub.fidelity; color = col, markersize = 9)
end
axislegend(ax; framevisible = false, position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

This has a direct practical consequence, and it is why `compare` never fits on
a subsample of your table however large it is: subsampling penalises private
engines far more than public ones, and can reverse the very ranking the
comparison exists to establish.

## Evaluation: what the numbers mean {#evaluation-what-the-numbers-mean}

Three families of metric, measuring three things that can disagree — and the
disagreements are the informative part. High fidelity with low utility usually
means the marginals are right and the relationships between columns are not.

### Fidelity — does it look like the original?

```{julia}
f = fidelity_score(adult_sub, diff_syn)
@printf("aggregate            %.4f   (0 = perfect)\n", f.aggregate)
@printf("correlation score    %.4f\n", f.correlation_score)
@printf("columns in corr term %d, excluded %d\n",
        length(f.correlation_columns), length(f.correlation_excluded))
sort(DataFrame(column = collect(keys(f.column_scores)),
               score  = collect(values(f.column_scores))), :score, rev = true)
```

Every number here is a **distance**, so lower is better. Numeric columns are
compared by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic — the largest gap between the two
empirical CDFs — and categoricals by total variation distance, half the sum of
absolute differences in level probabilities. Both are bounded in $[0,1]$, which
is what makes them commensurable enough to aggregate.

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "The KS statistic is the widest vertical gap between the two empirical CDFs."
v_real = sort(Float64.(adult_sub.age))
v_syn  = sort(Float64.(diff_syn.age))
grid = range(minimum(v_real), maximum(v_real); length = 400)
ecdf_at(v, g) = [count(<=(x), v) / length(v) for x in g]
Fr, Fs = ecdf_at(v_real, grid), ecdf_at(v_syn, grid)
k = argmax(abs.(Fr .- Fs))

fig = Figure(size = (680, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "age", ylabel = "F(age)",
          title = @sprintf("KS = %.4f", maximum(abs.(Fr .- Fs))))
lines!(ax, grid, Fr; color = PALETTE.real, linewidth = 2.5, label = "real")
lines!(ax, grid, Fs; color = PALETTE.synth, linewidth = 2.5, label = "synthetic")
lines!(ax, [grid[k], grid[k]], [Fr[k], Fs[k]];
       color = :black, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash, label = "KS")
axislegend(ax; framevisible = false, position = :rb)
fig
```

The correlation term compares **Spearman** rather than Pearson correlation,
deliberately: rank correlation is invariant to the marginal shapes already
scored by the per-column terms, so the two parts measure different things
instead of double-counting. Constant columns are excluded from it and reported
in `correlation_excluded` — their ranks never vary, so any correlation
involving them is undefined.

Two related measures catch what per-column scores cannot:

```{julia}
js  = jensen_shannon(adult_sub, diff_syn)
pme = pairwise_marginal_error(adult_sub, diff_syn; order = 2)
@printf("Jensen–Shannon (mean)      %.4f\n", js.mean)
@printf("pairwise marginal error    %.4f  over %d pairs\n", pme.mean, pme.n_pairs)
@printf("worst pair                 %s  (%.4f)\n", string(pme.worst_pair), pme.worst_score)
```

`pairwise_marginal_error` discretizes the columns and compares every *pair's*
joint distribution. A generator that got every marginal perfect but sampled
columns independently would score near zero on fidelity's per-column terms and
badly here. That is exactly the failure mode worth catching.

### Utility — is it useful downstream?

```{julia}
u = utility_tstr(adult_sub, diff_syn, :income; rng = MersenneTwister(51))
DataFrame(task = [string(u.task)], synth_score = [u.synth_score],
          real_score = [u.real_score], ratio = [u.ratio])
```

Train on synthetic, test on real. Gradient-boosted trees are fitted twice —
once on synthetic data, once on real — and both are scored against the same
held-out real data. Classification is scored by macro-averaged F1, regression
by RMSE.

The ratio is the number to look at, and it is the most direct evidence that a
synthetic table is fit for purpose. It is also the most sensitive to dependence
structure, which is exactly what generators find hardest.

### Privacy — how close does it sit to real records?

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Distance to closest real record. Mass piled at zero would mean the generator is reproducing records."
d_diff = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], diff_syn[1:3000, :])
d_copy = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], adult_sub[1:3000, :])   # worst case

@printf("synthetic : median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_diff.median, d_diff.exact_matches)
@printf("real vs itself : median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_copy.median, d_copy.exact_matches)

fig = Figure(size = (680, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "distance to closest real record", ylabel = "density",
          title = "DCR distribution")
hist!(ax, d_diff.dcr; bins = 50, color = (PALETTE.synth, 0.7), normalization = :pdf)
vlines!(ax, [d_diff.median]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2)
fig
```

The second line is the degenerate case: a table compared against itself has
every distance zero and every row an exact match. That is what a generator
which memorised its input would look like.

Treat DCR as a smoke test, not a guarantee. It measures one sample rather than
bounding all of them: a good DCR does not substitute for a privacy budget, and
a formal budget does not require a good DCR. Note also that it is
$O(n_{\text{synth}} \times n_{\text{real}})$, so evaluate it on a subsample of
large tables — as done above.

## Choosing an engine, empirically

Here is the payoff. At the start we hypothesised which engine would suit each
dataset. `compare` settles it: it fits each engine to your own table, repeats
over several seeds, and reports the mean and spread.

```{julia}
function bench(df, target; n = 4_000, seeds = 3)
    sub = df[1:min(n, nrow(df)), :]
    compare([CopulaGenerator(), CopulaGenerator(:gaussian),
             MSTGenerator(), DPCopulaGenerator()], sub;
            metrics = (fidelity = (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate,
                       utility  = (r, s) -> utility_tstr(r, s, target;
                                                rng = MersenneTwister(61)).ratio),
            n_seeds = seeds,
            privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0),
            rng = MersenneTwister(62))
end

results = vcat(
    DataFrame(bench(german, :credit_risk)) |> d -> (d.dataset .= "German Credit"; d),
    DataFrame(bench(wine, :quality))       |> d -> (d.dataset .= "Wine";          d),
    DataFrame(bench(adult_sub, :income))   |> d -> (d.dataset .= "Adult";         d),
)
select(results, :dataset, :generator, :metric, :mean, :sd, :fit_secs, :ok)
```

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Utility ratio by engine and dataset, with seed-to-seed spread. The winner changes."
util = filter(r -> r.metric === :utility && r.ok, results)
gens = unique(util.generator)
dsets = unique(util.dataset)

fig = Figure(size = (860, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "TSTR ratio (higher is better)",
          xticks = (1:length(dsets), dsets), title = "utility by engine")
w = 0.8 / length(gens)
cols = [PALETTE.real, PALETTE.synth, PALETTE.accent, "#8E6C88"]
for (gi, g) in enumerate(gens)
    xs = Float64[]; ys = Float64[]; es = Float64[]
    for (di, d) in enumerate(dsets)
        r = filter(x -> x.generator == g && x.dataset == d, util)
        isempty(r) && continue
        push!(xs, di + (gi - (length(gens) + 1) / 2) * w)
        push!(ys, r.mean[1]); push!(es, isnan(r.sd[1]) ? 0.0 : r.sd[1])
    end
    barplot!(ax, xs, ys; width = w * 0.9, color = (cols[gi], 0.85), label = g)
    errorbars!(ax, xs, ys, es; color = :black, whiskerwidth = 6)
end
hlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash)
axislegend(ax; framevisible = false, position = :lt, labelsize = 9)
fig
```

### What the hypotheses got wrong

**`CopulaGenerator(:beta)` wins on fidelity on all three datasets**, including
the categorical-heavy one that `MSTGenerator` was supposed to own — 0.025
against MST's 0.100 on German Credit, and 0.010 against 0.051 on Adult. The
reasoning behind that hypothesis was not silly; it was just not tested. MST is
built for *private* discrete synthesis, and here it is paying for a privacy
guarantee that the copula is not providing at all. Comparing a private engine
against a public one on fidelity alone measures the cost of privacy, not the
quality of the algorithm.

That is the honest summary of the private engines throughout: the gap is the
price of the guarantee. It is worth paying when you need it and pure loss when
you do not, which is why the choice is yours and not a heuristic's.

**But a ranking really does flip**, and it is the one visible above between the
two copula families:

| Dataset | `:beta` utility | `:gaussian` utility | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| German Credit | ~1.34 | ~0.79 | `:beta` |
| Adult | ~1.03 | ~0.64 | `:beta` |
| Wine | ~0.89 | ~1.22 | `:gaussian` |

Wine is the all-continuous dataset, and a Gaussian copula is a natural fit for
it — a single correlation matrix is close to the right model. On the two tables
with many categorical columns, the arbitrary level ordering produces
non-monotone structure that only the nonparametric Beta copula can represent,
exactly as [Step 3](#step-3-categoricals-and-why-beta-beats-gaussian)
predicted. The default is `:beta` because most tabular data has categoricals in
it, not because it dominates.

### Read the ratios sceptically

Several utility ratios above are **greater than 1**, which would say a model
trained on synthetic data beats one trained on real data. Take that as a
warning about the measurement rather than a result. At these sample sizes —
1,000 rows for German Credit — the train-on-synthetic and train-on-real scores
are both noisy, and their ratio is noisier still. A generator cannot add
information that was not in the data.

That is why the error bars are drawn and why `compare` warns below three seeds.
Where the intervals overlap, the difference in means is not evidence of
anything — and a single-seed run would have reported a confident winner anyway.

`compare` isolates failures too: an engine that errors is reported with
`ok = false` and its message while the others continue. A diffusion model that
diverges overnight should not cost you the comparison of everything else.

## Practical guidance

**Start with `CopulaGenerator()`.** It fits in seconds, handles mixed types
well, and gives you a baseline that everything else has to beat. Reaching for a
diffusion model first is a common way to spend an afternoon discovering that
the copula was fine.

**Give each engine a fair configuration before comparing.** Engines differ
enormously in how much they depend on their hyperparameters. Comparing a tuned
copula against an undertrained diffusion model measures your patience, not the
methods.

**Use at least three seeds.** Below that the reported standard deviation is
meaningless, and `compare` warns.

**Do not subsample for fitting** unless you mean to. Private engines lose far
more from it than public ones.

**Check utility, not just fidelity.** Distributional similarity is easy to game
by sampling columns independently; downstream utility is not.

**If you need a formal guarantee, use a private engine from the start.** DCR on
a non-private generator's output is a smoke test, not a substitute — and
retrofitting privacy is not possible, because the model already saw the data.

## References

The engines implement published algorithms, cross-checked against reference
implementations rather than the papers alone. The full bibliography, including
the specific points where this package departs from a paper, is in
[`references/REFERENCES.md`](https://github.com/mthelm85/DataMimic.jl/blob/main/references/REFERENCES.md).

- **Sklar (1959)**; **Nelsen**, *An Introduction to Copulas*, 2nd ed. (2006) —
  copula theory behind `CopulaGenerator`.
- **Kotelnikov, Baranchuk, Rubachev & Babenko (2023)**, *TabDDPM: Modelling
  Tabular Data with Diffusion Models*, ICML —
  [arXiv:2209.15421](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15421).
- **Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)**, *Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*,
  NeurIPS; **Nichol & Dhariwal (2021)** for the cosine schedule;
  **Hoogeboom et al. (2021)** for multinomial diffusion.
- **McKenna, Miklau & Sheldon (2021)**, *Winning the NIST Contest*, JPC 11(3);
  **McKenna, Sheldon & Miklau (2019)**, *Graphical-model based estimation and
  inference for differential privacy*, ICML — `MSTGenerator`.
- **Dwork, Talwar, Thakurta & Zhang (2014)**, *Analyze Gauss*, STOC —
  `DPCopulaGenerator`.
- **Abadi et al. (2016)**, *Deep Learning with Differential Privacy*, CCS;
  **Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019)** for the Rényi accountant;
  **Goodfellow (2015)** and **Li et al. (2021)**,
  [arXiv:2110.05679](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05679), for ghost clipping.
